REASONS FOR DECISION

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Haiti, is claiming refugee protection under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
DETERMINATION

[2] The panel determines that the claimant did not establish that there is a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that, on a balance of probabilities, she would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, a risk to her life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if she had to return to her country.
SUMMARY OF ALLEGATIONS

[3] The claimant was married on XXXX XXXX, 2016.

[4] Her husband was a technician who worked on XXXX for a company named XXXX XXXX, a subsidiary of XXXX.

[5] In early 2017, her husband was threatened.

[23] Asked to explain why, in her BOC Form, this incident was placed after January 2017, whereas according to her testimony it took place in late 2016, the claimant explained that she was in shock when she wrote the account because it was right after her husband's murder. She added that, since then, she has had some time to collect herself (as the claimant put it) and that she was telling the panel her story.

[24] The panel rejects that explanation.

[27] The panel is also aware that the claimant was seven months pregnant when she arrived in Canada. However, this cannot explain her credibility problems.

[28] But there is more regarding her and her husband being in a car that was intercepted by criminals.

[29] The claimant was asked to sketch the streets where she was allegedly intercepted by the criminals.4 The claimant explained that it was about 9:00 p.m., when her car was stopped behind another car at a red light. The criminals arrived from a one-way street perpendicular to the two-way street where the claimant's car was waiting for the traffic light to change.

[30] The claimant was asked how the criminals could know that her car would be stopped at that particular spot in order to intercept them. She explained that the criminals might have followed them and taken an alternate route at some point in order to intercept them there.

[31] The panel rejects that explanation.

[32] The panel does not believe, on a balance of probabilities, that the criminals would have known exactly when the claimant and her husband would arrive at an intersection in order to intercept and attempt to threaten her.

[33] For the reasons given, the panel does not believe that the claimant and her husband were intercepted by criminals and, accordingly, that these criminals would be looking for her because she can identify them as her husband's killers.
Threats from criminals in February 2017

[34] The claimant testified that, one day on a weekend in February 2017, she accompanied her husband while he worked because she had nothing else to do. He had to go to XXXX XXXX to repair or install XXXX. She had to urge her husband to let her accompany him because it is a dangerous area. They were threatened by criminals in the area. The criminals wanted money and took the equipment in the truck. The criminals said that if they wanted to work in XXXX XXXX again, they needed to bring money. The claimant alleges that it is because she saw these criminals that day that they could consider her a witness to her husband's murder.

[35] Asked to explain why she did not mention the above information in her BOC Form, the claimant stated that she was in shock from her husband's murder when she wrote her account. She added that it was only once she was over the shock that she started remembering what had happened.

[36] The panel rejects this explanation. The panel is of the opinion that once she was over the shock, the claimant could have amended her BOC Form, which she did not do. The panel draws a negative inference from the fact that the claimant amended the BOC Form the day of her hearing but failed to state that she and her husband had been threatened when he was in XXXX XXXX to work on XXXX and that her husband could not return to work in the area without giving money to the criminals.

[37] The panel therefore does not believe that the claimant saw the criminals in XXXX XXXX.

subthemes.text:
[44] Before the break, she stated that she did not fully understand the panel's question, and after the break, she seemed to state that she had exaggerated her knowledge when she testified the second time about her knowledge of the identity of the criminals. The panel is of the opinion that the claimant was trying to get herself out of an awkward situation.

[45] Her lawyer also asked her how she was feeling at the hearing. The claimant responded that she was both emotional and a little stressed by the questions, that she found it difficult to relive her husband's death and that she felt uncomfortable.

[46] The panel empathizes with the feelings expressed by the claimant. Nevertheless, the contradiction regarding her knowledge of the criminals' identity undermines her credibility.

[47] The claimant testified that the criminals took her husband's body to the hospital and then tried to flee, but that they were arrested by a security guard. The panel is of the opinion, on a balance of probabilities, that it is implausible that criminals linked to a murder would take the dead body of someone they had just killed to a hospital and risk being identified and arrested.

[48] The panel therefore does not believe that the claimant's husband was killed by criminals who had threatened him because of his work as a XXXX XXXX.

REASONS FOR DECISION

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Haiti, is claiming refugee protection under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
DETERMINATION

[2] The panel determines that the claimant did not establish that there is a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that, on a balance of probabilities, she would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, a risk to her life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if she had to return to her country.
SUMMARY OF ALLEGATIONS
[3] The claimant was married on XXXX XXXX, 2016.
[4] Her husband was a technician who worked on XXXX for a company named XXXX XXXX, a subsidiary of XXXX.
[5] In early 2017, her husband was threatened.
[6] One night, their car was intercepted by armed criminals, who demanded money.
[7] On XXXX XXXX, 2017, the claimant went to the United States for a check-up relating to her pregnancy.
[8] On August 6, 2017, the threats became serious and her husband's car was vandalized.
[9] On August 7, 2017, an armed group went to the house and her husband had to give money to them.
[10] On August 9, 2017, the claimant talked to her husband for the last time.
[11] That day, he asked his servant to leave the gate open because he was on his way.
[12] On XXXX XXXX, 2017, he died.
[13] According to the explanations, he was already dead when he was taken to the hospital. His arms were broken and he had bruises over most of his body.
[14] The two people who took him to the hospital were arrested. They are in prison and an investigation is under way.

[15] The claimant fears returning to Haiti because she would be considered a troublesome witness because she could help the police find the criminals, two of whom are in prison.
IDENTITY

[16] The claimant's identity was established to the panel's satisfaction with a copy of her passport that was entered into evidence.1
ANALYSIS
[17] The determinative issue is whether the claimant is credible with respect to the fact that she knows her husband's murderers because she has seen them before and could therefore identify them.
[18] The panel does not find the claimant credible, for the following reasons.

[19] Before proceeding with its analysis, the panel would like to mention that the claimant is well educated, that she did not require a translation of her Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), and that she testified directly in French. There was absolutely no indication during the hearing that she did not understand the proceedings before the panel.
Car intercepted by criminals

[20] In her BOC Form, the claimant begins her allegations about the threats from the criminals as follows:
[translation]
My husband and I were always true partners. We talked about everything and anything. In early 2017, he started telling me that he was receiving threats through anonymous calls. The callers knew all about him, and if he was not willing to give them what they asked, he should avoid their area as much as possible....2

[21] The next paragraph starts with the following:
[translation]
One night, these armed criminals intercepted our vehicle and demanded money....3
[22] At the hearing, the claimant testified that around November or December 2016, their car had been intercepted by criminals in the XXXX XXXX XXXX area.

[23] Asked to explain why, in her BOC Form, this incident was placed after January 2017, whereas according to her testimony it took place in late 2016, the claimant explained that she was in shock when she wrote the account because it was right after her husband's murder. She added that, since then, she has had some time to collect herself (as the claimant put it) and that she was telling the panel her story.
[24] The panel rejects that explanation.

[25] First of all, the claimant has been in Canada for nearly a year, she speaks French, and she is represented by an experienced lawyer. The panel is of the opinion that all the pieces were in place for her to be able to make the necessary amendments and ensure that her story reflects her experiences as much as possible. Furthermore, the panel draws a negative inference from the fact that the claimant stated under oath at the beginning of the hearing that all of the information in her BOC Form was true, complete and correct, yet as soon as she is confronted with a contradiction, she states that, since coming to Canada, she has had time to collect herself.
[26] The panel also notes that the claimant did not specify in her BOC Form that these criminals were from XXXX XXXX XXXX.
[27] The panel is also aware that the claimant was seven months pregnant when she arrived in Canada. However, this cannot explain her credibility problems.
[28] But there is more regarding her and her husband being in a car that was intercepted by criminals.

[29] The claimant was asked to sketch the streets where she was allegedly intercepted by the criminals.4 The claimant explained that it was about 9:00 p.m., when her car was stopped behind another car at a red light. The criminals arrived from a one-way street perpendicular to the two-way street where the claimant's car was waiting for the traffic light to change.

[30] The claimant was asked how the criminals could know that her car would be stopped at that particular spot in order to intercept them. She explained that the criminals might have followed them and taken an alternate route at some point in order to intercept them there.
[31] The panel rejects that explanation.

[32] The panel does not believe, on a balance of probabilities, that the criminals would have known exactly when the claimant and her husband would arrive at an intersection in order to intercept and attempt to threaten her.

[33] For the reasons given, the panel does not believe that the claimant and her husband were intercepted by criminals and, accordingly, that these criminals would be looking for her because she can identify them as her husband's killers.
Threats from criminals in February 2017

[34] The claimant testified that, one day on a weekend in February 2017, she accompanied her husband while he worked because she had nothing else to do. He had to go to XXXX XXXX to repair or install XXXX. She had to urge her husband to let her accompany him because it is a dangerous area. They were threatened by criminals in the area. The criminals wanted money and took the equipment in the truck. The criminals said that if they wanted to work in XXXX XXXX again, they needed to bring money. The claimant alleges that it is because she saw these criminals that day that they could consider her a witness to her husband's murder.

[35] Asked to explain why she did not mention the above information in her BOC Form, the claimant stated that she was in shock from her husband's murder when she wrote her account. She added that it was only once she was over the shock that she started remembering what had happened.

[36] The panel rejects this explanation. The panel is of the opinion that once she was over the shock, the claimant could have amended her BOC Form, which she did not do. The panel draws a negative inference from the fact that the claimant amended the BOC Form the day of her hearing but failed to state that she and her husband had been threatened when he was in XXXX XXXX to work on XXXX and that her husband could not return to work in the area without giving money to the criminals.

[37] The panel therefore does not believe that the claimant saw the criminals in XXXX XXXX.
Her husband's killers
[38] First of all, the claimant testified that she did not know whether the murderers were the criminals from XXXX XXXX or the ones from XXXX XXXX XXXX.
[39] Later on during the hearing, she testified that the criminals who had been arrested at the hospital were from XXXX XXXX.
[40] When asked to explain the contradiction, the claimant stated that the first question she answered had not been very clear.
[41] After the break, her lawyer returned to this part of her testimony.
[42] The claimant explained that she had wanted to seem more sure of herself than she really was when she answered that the criminals were from XXXX XXXX.
[43] The panel rejects these explanations.

[44] Before the break, she stated that she did not fully understand the panel's question, and after the break, she seemed to state that she had exaggerated her knowledge when she testified the second time about her knowledge of the identity of the criminals. The panel is of the opinion that the claimant was trying to get herself out of an awkward situation.

[45] Her lawyer also asked her how she was feeling at the hearing. The claimant responded that she was both emotional and a little stressed by the questions, that she found it difficult to relive her husband's death and that she felt uncomfortable.
[46] The panel empathizes with the feelings expressed by the claimant. Nevertheless, the contradiction regarding her knowledge of the criminals' identity undermines her credibility.

[47] The claimant testified that the criminals took her husband's body to the hospital and then tried to flee, but that they were arrested by a security guard. The panel is of the opinion, on a balance of probabilities, that it is implausible that criminals linked to a murder would take the dead body of someone they had just killed to a hospital and risk being identified and arrested.

[48] The panel therefore does not believe that the claimant's husband was killed by criminals who had threatened him because of his work as a XXXX XXXX.
Documents submitted as evidence

[49] The panel received in evidence an extract from the registry of the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX dated XXXX XXXX, 2017;5 a notarized statement from three people;6 a statement from the claimant's sister-in-law;7 a statement from her aunt in Canada;8 and a letter from XXXX XXXX, the employer.9 These documents are insufficient to make credible testimony that is essentially not credible. Therefore, the panel cannot give them any probative value.

[50] Three documents were filed in evidence in relation to the death of the claimant's husband at the hands of the criminals who had threatened him because of his work.10 The panel cannot give any probative value to them either, because the claimant was not credible with respect to the incidents that led to her husband's murder due to his work.
CONCLUSION

[51] For these reasons, the panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

[52] Consequently, the panel rejects the refugee protection claim filed by XXXX XXXX XXXX.
